title: Pay for the Reasoning Once
excerpt: A coding agent can scaffold a new service from a prompt, but it pays for the same reasoning again on every run. A better split lets the agent do the expensive reasoning once, freezes that reasoning into a deterministic Nx generator, and has skills call the generator as a tool. This post argues for that split, shows what knowledge is worth freezing, and explains where freezing stops paying.

toc.value: The cost of the nth scaffold

title: Technical Debt Needs Repayment Terms
excerpt: On many teams, "technical debt" is a label that ends a discussion. Someone says it, everyone agrees to pay it back later, and nobody has to say what the repayment will cost. Mature teams use debt on purpose to close a feedback loop sooner, inside a plan that already includes the payback. This post is about the difference, and about why a fixed percentage of capacity for paydown is not the same as a plan.

toc.value: Where the fixed percentage goes wrong

title: The Feature I Never Had to Ship: Open-Closed by Composition
excerpt: A retry library got a request it was never designed for: poll forever. The library had no infinite option, and it did not need one. Stopping was already a predicate that the caller passed in, so a one-line predicate met the need with no change to the retry loop. This post is about that design choice, what it costs, and why shared platform tools need the same shape.

toc.value: The same shape at platform scale

title: What a Small App Taught Me About Domain-Driven Design
excerpt: Fin is a small household finance app that I built to practice domain-driven design. The tactical building blocks held up well. The harder questions were the ones the design left open: where one model ends and the next begins, how two aggregates change together, what an error means, who owns an identity, and where a rule runs. This post looks at each question, what it cost, and what I would do next time.

toc.value: What the tactical design got right
Draw bounded contexts before the vision outgrows the model
Aggregate boundaries show their cost in cross-aggregate flows
Persistence ignorance leaks in small ways
Elegant rules can hide scaling costs
The design document I would write now

title: Rotating Broker Certificates Without a Gap
excerpt: Certificate-based AMQPS removes the broker password, but only if rotation is routine and nobody notices it. This post covers RabbitMQ with the cluster operator, NServiceBus endpoints that authenticate with a client certificate, and how to rotate client certificates, broker certificates, and the root that signs them both without dropping a consumer.

toc.value: Three things rotate, on three schedules
Client certificates: the overlap is the guarantee
Restarts that do not drop consumers
The broker certificate: trust the issuer, not the leaf
The root: two roots for a while

title: End-to-End TLS Is a Chain of Handoffs
excerpt: End-to-end TLS through an edge gateway and a service mesh is not one certificate. It is a chain of handoffs, and each layer must trust the next one with its own copy of the material. This post covers the pattern with cert-manager, External Secrets Operator, Key Vault, Application Gateway, and an Istio ingress gateway, and the lessons that only show up at renewal time.

toc.value: The edge must trust what the ingress presents
Inside the cluster, the mesh takes over
Renewal is where the chain breaks

title: The Price of Going Private
excerpt: Private endpoints move a managed service off the public internet and onto the provider backbone. The security case takes one sentence. The bill arrives in DNS, in CI agents that can no longer reach anything, in debugging sessions that start with a VPN, and in the invoice. This post walks through each cost and when the trade is worth it.

toc.value: Debugging starts with a network path

title: Custody, Not Cryptography: What Customer-Managed Keys Actually Change
excerpt: Azure already encrypts every byte at rest with AES-256. Customer-managed keys do not make that encryption stronger. They change who holds the key that unlocks the keys, which gives the operator an audited revocation switch and makes the key vault a tier-0 dependency. This post covers the model, the decision, and the per-service integration work that the one-line policy hides.

toc.value: One policy, a different mechanism per service

title: Reconcilers Without Standing Privilege
excerpt: Infrastructure as code stops where a provider stops, and the state past that line still drifts. The Kubernetes reflex is to write a controller that converges it forever. This post argues that reconciler work does not need a controller that holds long-lived privilege in the cluster. The reconciler runs on demand instead, under the operator's own short-lived identity, so its access lasts only for the run.

toc.value: A safety model for the person who holds the keys
When a standing controller is the right answer
Requests that would undo the design

title: Living With Deny by Default in a Service Mesh
excerpt: A floor that denies every call by default in an Istio mesh is one small policy. The work is everything after it: how a new service gets its first allowed call, how an engineer tells a mesh denial from an application error, and how a cluster's worth of allow rules stays readable. This post covers the floor, workload identity, AuthorizationPolicy, and the habits that make deny by default livable.

toc.value: The floor is one empty policy

title: The Network Floor Under an Identity Mesh
excerpt: A private virtual network is open east-west by default, and "it is inside the VNet" does not mean isolated. Even with an identity-aware service mesh, the coarse L3/L4 network still has a job: it is the floor that holds when the assumptions of the richer layer break. This post covers why, what closing the default costs, and the stateful-routing mistakes that silently drop traffic.

toc.value: Two layers that authorize different things
Closing the default sends a bill
Forced egress is one line of intent and a hard packet problem
Put invariants where nothing can violate them

title: Split the Environment Along the Network Boundary
excerpt: A design for per-pull-request environments made sense until the network went private. This post walks through the reversal: why the original premises failed, how the lifecycle now splits at the network boundary between CI and a controller in the cluster, and how a pull-request label states what data an environment needs.

toc.value: The pull request states what data it needs

title: One CI Identity for Two Control Planes
excerpt: A pipeline acts on two systems: the cloud where it pushes images and reads secrets, and the build platform itself where it restores feeds and cancels runs. This post explains how one secret-less service connection, owned by Terraform, can be the identity for both, why it should replace personal access tokens and the ambient build token, and why its permissions still live in two places.

toc.value: One login, then the scripts fan out

title: Least Privilege Has a Clock
excerpt: A deploy needs the right to change a database schema for a few seconds. So why does the internet-facing process that serves traffic hold that right for weeks? Scope dangerous capabilities by phase as well as by principal: give migrations their own identity and their own lifecycle.

toc.value: Migrate on boot, or migrate as a phase
Where the split is actually enforced

title: Nothing Holds a Secret: Identity Instead of Keys
excerpt: A connection string turns anyone who holds it into anyone. This post explains why a platform can ban resource keys and connection strings outright, how workload identity federation replaces them with a chain of short-lived proofs, and how to handle the places where federation is impossible without giving up the principle.

toc.value: The exception: a smaller secret, not a bigger key
Every credential is one of a few classes

title: Designing a Small Language for Releases
excerpt: Promotion logic tends to spread across bash scripts until nobody can say what a release will do. Treating the build-to-deploy contract as a small language, with one evaluator, explicit referential checks, and deliberate boundaries, keeps it readable and testable. This post is about the design discipline behind that language, not only its syntax.

toc.value: Name the parts, and arguments go away

title: Release Binding: How a Built Digest Becomes a Running Deploy
excerpt: For years, a naming convention connected builds to deploys: one project, one image, one chart, one GitOps folder, all with the same name. Then sidecars, fan-outs, and cross-project images appeared, and the convention could not express them. This post explains how a small catalog-and-binding model replaced it, and why only fresh artifacts should ever move.

title: One Registry for Production: Promoting Images Across a Trust Boundary
excerpt: When production can pull images from only one private registry, an ErrImagePull on a public image is the design working, not a bug. This post walks through an exclusive-registry policy: what it buys, what it costs, how images cross from a development tenant to a production tenant, and how to debug the chain when it breaks.

title: Resize on Collisions, Not Load Factor
excerpt: Most hash tables grow when they are 75 percent full. That rule assumes keys spread evenly across the table. An experiment with skewed and clustered keys shows what happens when they do not, and what changes when the table grows on the cost it actually pays, which is the number of slots an insert must check.

toc.value: Measure the cost you care about

title: Why a Monorepo Still Publishes Packages

This post explains why that reference can be the wrong choice, how a package boundary cuts the build graph and lets each consumer adopt changes on its own schedule, and why the merge gate asks the feed a question instead of reading the diff.

title: CI Is a Framework, Not a Library
excerpt: Every new service checklist has an "add CI/CD" step, and that step is a warning sign. When each repository assembles its own pipeline, the pipeline drifts in every repository. A better model lets CI own the control flow and call a small, stable vocabulary of target names that each project implements.

excerpt: Google Analytics was too much for my needs. I wanted lightweight analytics that respect privacy, with full control. So I built a fully automated Plausible deployment with AKS, Helm, cert-manager, and Azure Front Door. This post shows how it works.

excerpt: A short API outage became a full incident. The system did not fail. Every client retried at the same time. Bad retries do more than add noise. They can stop healthy services, overload your infrastructure, and change short transient errors into cascading failures. This post shows what smarter retries look like and how to design them for real-world resilience.
